inquiry.title: Illustrative Anschluss Consolidation Inquiry
inquiry.question: Conditional on Nazi Germany permanently ending external expansion after the March 1938 Anschluss, what is the political-territorial outcome by March 1948?
inquiry.resolution_criteria: Classify the status of Hitler's regime and German control of Austria in March 1948.
inquiry.scope: European political-territorial outcome; not a welfare evaluation or an endorsement of Nazi objectives.
inquiry.ethical_note: Strategic success is analytically distinct from human welfare. Every modeled branch retains severe Nazi persecution unless separately changed.
limitations: All numerical priors and likelihoods are illustrative elicitation values, not a completed scholarly estimate.
The antecedent changes a central feature of Hitler's ideology and therefore has substantial actor-coherence uncertainty.
The three hypotheses compress many possible successions, coups, negotiated settlements, and conflicts.
No source-provenance graph or independently calibrated expert panel has yet populated this example.

hypotheses.label: Hitler's regime retains Germany and Austria
hypotheses.description: Hitler remains the effective head of the Nazi regime and Austria remains incorporated through March 1948.

hypotheses.label: A successor regime retains Austria
hypotheses.description: Hitler's personal regime ends, but a German successor state continues to control Austria.

hypotheses.label: Germany loses control of Austria
hypotheses.description: War, negotiated reversal, internal collapse, or foreign intervention restores Austrian separation by March 1948.

models.label: Diplomatic-security model
assumptions: Britain and France prefer avoiding war if expansion genuinely stops.
No external coalition forms solely to reverse the Anschluss.

models.label: Political-economy model
assumptions: Rearmament and foreign-exchange constraints force material policy changes.
Economic stress threatens leadership durability more than the border settlement itself.

models.label: Institutional-succession model
assumptions: The personalized polycratic regime contains material succession risk.
German and Austrian integration can outlast Hitler personally.

evidence.description: The European powers did not use military force to reverse the Anschluss at the time.
distortions: Short-run nonintervention does not guarantee ten-year acceptance.

evidence.description: The regime rapidly incorporated Austrian political, monetary, and administrative institutions.
distortions: Administrative control is not equivalent to durable legitimacy.

evidence.description: German rearmament had produced serious import and foreign-exchange constraints by 1938.
distortions: Authoritarian regimes can redirect, conceal, or survive severe economic imbalances.

evidence.description: The Nazi state concentrated authority around Hitler while maintaining rival and overlapping institutions.
distortions: Institutional rivalry can strengthen a dictator before it destabilizes succession.

challenges.description: A permanent end to expansion conflicts with Hitler's repeatedly stated ideological objectives; an illness, restraint mechanism, or different leader may be a more coherent intervention.
Economic consolidation requires reducing or redirecting the mobilization system on which Nazi legitimacy and elite competition increasingly depended.
The inquiry has not yet modeled Soviet, Italian, Japanese, Polish, Czechoslovak, or colonial dynamics as endogenous responses.

translations.warning: The terms overlap but are not interchangeable.
